# status: "assumption" = chosen for plausibility, not calibrated to data.

  status: assumption

    baseline: [annual, quarterly]

  recent_quarters: 4    # "recent" = latest 4 origin quarters (1 annual period)
  status: assumption

  n_reps: 30
  commit: 30cc7a8402f29713d3f53861e42b092cbc6946f1   # thierrymoudiki/ChainLadder (fork of mages/ChainLadder)
  configs:              # blog setting first; the rest are variants incl. the package default (factor features), all scored on the same replications

    rf_raw_numeric: {learner: ranger, features: numeric, transform: none}
    rf_raw_both: {learner: ranger, features: both, transform: none}

    svm_raw_factor: {learner: svm, features: factor, transform: none}
  status: assumption

  recon_automation:
    description: Automated daily position/cash reconciliation against prime-broker statements
    annual_cost_usd: 400000          # assumption; range 250k - 600k
    lag_shift:

    annual_cost_usd: 700000          # assumption; range 400k - 1.2M
    lag_shift:

      nav_error: {slow_meanlog: -0.3}
      unauthorized_trading: {slow_meanlog: -0.8, w_fast: 0.15}
    status: assumption

    lambda: 60                       # events / quarter at exposure 1; range 30 - 120
    lag: {w_fast: 0.85, p_fast: 0.80, slow_meanlog: 0.5, slow_sdlog: 0.8}
    severity: {meanlog: 7.8, sdlog: 1.2, p_tail: 0.03, tail_q: 0.95, xi: 0.2, beta: 8000, lag_elasticity: 0.02}
    status: assumption
  nav_error:                         # Basel: EDPM / Clients, Products & Business Practices
    lambda: 6                        # range 3 - 15
    lag: {w_fast: 0.50, p_fast: 0.40, slow_meanlog: 1.5, slow_sdlog: 0.8}
    severity: {meanlog: 10.3, sdlog: 1.4, p_tail: 0.05, tail_q: 0.95, xi: 0.3, beta: 80000, lag_elasticity: 0.05}
    status: assumption
  unauthorized_trading:              # Basel: Internal Fraud (incl. limit and mandate breaches)
    lambda: 0.3                      # ~1.2 per year; range 0.1 - 0.8
    lag: {w_fast: 0.10, p_fast: 0.30, slow_meanlog: 2.0, slow_sdlog: 0.9}
    severity: {meanlog: 12.4, sdlog: 1.6, p_tail: 0.08, tail_q: 0.90, xi: 0.6, beta: 1500000, lag_elasticity: 0.08}

scenarios:
  baseline: {}
  heavy_tail_shock:
    injected_events:                 # absolute-dollar events added to the baseline
      - {type: unauthorized_trading, origin: 12, lag: 15, severity: 60000000}
      - {type: unauthorized_trading, origin: 20, lag: 22, severity: 40000000}

What the tests cover:

Triangle construction reconciles exactly to the event-level data (counts and amounts, quarterly and annual) and never leaks undiscovered events into the observed region.
The generator is deterministic for a seed, rejects invalid parameters, keeps lags non-negative under the control shift, injects shock events exactly, and the control-improvement shift reduces time remaining by the stated fraction measured from the later of the shift quarter and the origin (events originating after the shift are not collapsed to lag 0).
The negative-binomial scenario has the same mean count as Poisson but larger variance, and the reporting threshold removes only losses below it.
Estimators: the in-house chain-ladder matches the package on a dense triangle, tolerates empty development columns, never throws (errors become failed), and sparse triangles are reported as failed or suspect, never as silent zeros. The Mack implementation with empty-column handling reproduces ChainLadder::MackChainLadder on a dense triangle (IBNR and standard error), runs where the package stops, and a zero bootstrap estimate is flagged suspect. Bornhuetter-Ferguson, Benktander and the benchmark development pattern are checked for coherence (shares in [0, 1], Benktander between BF and chain-ladder, pattern matches simulation).
Scoring and control functions are checked against hand-computed values.
A replication run is identical on 1 and 2 cores.

title: Reproducibility and Limitations
text:
Caching and runtime
Pages cache their chunk results with Quarto freeze: auto; a page re-executes when its source changes. To force a full rebuild, delete _freeze/ and docs/. The heavy computation is not in the pages at all: it is in run_simulations.R, which took 7.9 minutes for the replications and 4 seconds for the control study and break-even on this run.

title: Reproducibility and Limitations
text:
Known limits of reproducibility

Bit-for-bit equality is expected only on the same platform and package versions. Floating-point and BLAS differences across machines can change low-order digits, and occasionally the optimiser path of the Clark fits.
The mlReserve fork is a moving target on GitHub; the pinned commit keeps the experiment fixed, but the fork could disappear.
Quarto and Typst versions affect rendering, not the numbers.

title: Reproducibility and Limitations
text:
Limitations and model risk
This project tests how estimation methods behave on data we generated. That is its strength (the true answer is known) and its main limitation (the answer holds only for this generator).

Key limitations

Synthetic, uncalibrated parameters. Frequencies, lag distributions, severities and control effects are assumptions chosen for plausibility. Different values would change the numbers, and may change which method works.
The generator and the methods share structure. Discovery lag is independent of origin period apart from the explicit scenarios, which is close to what chain-ladder assumes. Real loss databases have reporting-policy changes, system migrations and batch back-fills that create calendar-period effects the baseline does not contain.
Loss is booked in full at discovery. Real events also have payment and recovery development after discovery. This is a second triangle layer that is not modelled.
Event types are independent. In reality a market shock raises trade errors, NAV errors and unauthorized-position losses together.
Control effects are assumed. The savings come from a posited link between time undiscovered and loss size, and an assumed shift in the lag distribution. We have no evidence for either magnitude.
Frequency x severity ignores parameter uncertainty, so its intervals understate uncertainty by construction.
Interval method. Mack and Clark intervals use a lognormal approximation to the total; the bootstrap uses empirical quantiles. Other choices would change coverage numbers somewhat.
Annual vs. quarterly. Headline results use annual triangles because quarterly triangles are mostly unusable for the standard methods. A real firm with a long, dense history might do better at finer granularity.
One firm size. A $5B stylised firm; no other sizes were tested.
Poisson frequency, no clustering. Baseline counts are independent Poisson. Real operational-loss counts are overdispersed, and common-cause failures (for example a pricing feed that fails across many funds) produce batches of errors. The negative-binomial scenario adds overdispersion within an event type, but not clustering across types or across quarters.
No reporting threshold in the baseline. Real loss databases only record losses above a collection threshold, often $10k to $20k. The median simulated trade error is about $2.4k, so a real database would hold far fewer trade errors. A $10k threshold is run as a sensitivity scenario.
Some “method failures” are package limits, not method limits. ChainLadder::MackChainLadder() stops on triangles with empty development columns. Results with empty-column handling (factor 1) are reported next to the package results.
Frequency x severity donor sparsity. At long lags few observed events exist, so severities are resampled from the few that do (or from all events when none are nearby, which drops the lag uplift). A variant that pools severities and re-applies an estimated uplift is reported.
Every control result scales with the severity-growth parameter \(e\). With \(e = 0\) incurred loss is the same with and without the control (see Control Value).
Pure IBNR only. Loss is booked in full at discovery, so there is no development on events already known (provisions, recoveries, insurance). The terminology here is IBNR, not IBNER.
The benchmark development pattern is the generator’s own. The Bornhuetter-Ferguson variant with an external pattern shows what an accurate prior pattern buys; with a pattern that is itself wrong it would do worse, and the study does not test that.



What would change the conclusions







If we found…
Effect




Real unauthorized-trading events are far more frequent than ~1 per year
Standard methods become usable; the “cannot run” finding would weaken


Detection lags are stable over time in real data
The control-improvement failure matters less in practice


Loss size does not grow with time undiscovered
Control savings on expected loss largely disappear


Strong calendar-period effects in real data
All development methods would need an explicit calendar term


Losses arrive in clusters from a common failure
Chain-ladder variance is understated; Bornhuetter-Ferguson with a pooled pattern is preferred


Real collection threshold of $10k or more
The trade-error triangle is mostly empty and the standard methods have little to work with





What client data would replace each assumption







Synthetic parameter

Internal loss event database, trade-break and reconciliation logs


Discovery-lag distribution
Timestamps for occurrence, detection and booking in the loss database


Severity and tail
Booked losses; external data (for example consortium loss data) for the tail


Severity growth with lag
Cases where the same error type was found early and late

Before/after detection times around past control changes


Control cost
Vendor quotes and internal run cost


Firm size
Actual AUM and trade volumes





Use of the results
The numbers on this site are illustrations of method behaviour. They should not be quoted as estimates of any firm’s undiscovered losses or as a benchmark for the value of a particular control.

title: Experimental: ML Reserving
text:
An experimental comparator, kept out of the main Results page because it does not feed the conclusions on the Overview.






WarningExperimental, excluded from headline results



mlReserve() comes from a personal fork of the ChainLadder package (thierrymoudiki/ChainLadder, pinned to commit 30cc7a84, package version 0.2.22), not from CRAN. Its published evidence is a blog post using simulated insurance triangles. It was installed into an isolated library so the CRAN ChainLadder used on every other page is unaffected. Nothing on this page feeds the executive summary.



What it does
mlReserve() fits a machine-learning regression (here a random forest from ranger or a support vector machine from e1071) to the observed cells of a triangle, using origin and development period as features, and predicts the unobserved cells. It is a different idea from chain-ladder’s multiplicative development factors.


The test
Same simulated databases as the baseline validation (replications 1-30), annual dollar triangles, scored on the undiscovered loss inside the window. Four configurations are run and all are reported; none was chosen using the true values. The first is the setting used in the blog post. Point estimates only (no bootstrap intervals).

Reading the result

Every mlReserve configuration overestimates on the two event types where classical methods work. For NAV errors the closest configuration (mlReserve: rf_raw_both) has a median estimate/truth ratio of 3, against 0.84 for Mack. For trade errors the closest (mlReserve: rf_raw_both) is 20x the truth, against 0.96 for Mack.
Why: on a single triangle, the learner extrapolates an upward trend across origin years into cells that, in this simulator, are nearly fully developed. With 10 origin years there are only 55 training cells and tree/kernel learners have no development-factor structure to anchor them.
The blog’s asinh transform, applied to dollar values, gives a median ratio of 31 for trade errors, worse than the same learner with no transform in the cases we ran; it may be calibrated for much smaller numeric scales, and we did not test rescaling the data first.
Unauthorized trading: the closest configuration (mlReserve: svm_raw_numeric, median ratio 1.3) is not a useful comparison either way, since the truth is small and the estimates are highly dispersed.
We report the configurations after the fact for transparency; none was selected using the truth, and “closest” above describes this experiment, not a recommendation.

Taken together, this is a limited test, on one data-generating process, with no tuning, of an unreleased fork. It gives no support for using mlReserve here, and it does not show that the approach cannot work with more data or tuning.

title: Synthetic Data
text: All data are simulated. No internal or client loss data are used, and every parameter is an assumption chosen for plausibility, stored in params.yaml. The point is to have a known ground truth against which estimation methods can be scored, not to describe a real firm.

title: Synthetic Data
text:
Generator design
For each event type and origin quarter:

Count ~ Poisson(\(\lambda \times \text{exposure}\)), where exposure grows 1.0% per quarter. Counts are independent across quarters and event types, with no overdispersion or clustering (see Limitations).
Discovery lag (quarters): a mixture of a fast component (geometric) and a slow component (discretised lognormal).
Severity: lognormal body spliced to a generalised Pareto tail, then scaled by \((1 + e \times \text{lag})\), so events found later are larger. The uplift is linear in the lag (not compounding). It is a crude stand-in for an unauthorized position that keeps growing while hidden; \(e\) is the only mechanism by which a loss can change while undiscovered, so every dollar figure for controls on the Control Value page scales with it.
The loss is recorded in full at the discovery date.

The generator keeps the full square, so the true undiscovered loss is always known.

text:

text:
Scenarios







Scenario
What changes




Baseline
Stable detection, proportional development


Heavy-tail shock
Two very large unauthorized-trading losses injected: $60M originating in quarter 12 and discovered in quarter 27 (reported), and $40M originating in quarter 20 and discovered in quarter 42 (after the evaluation date, so undiscovered)


Control improvement
Applies to all three event types. For every event whose discovery quarter \(d\) is after the change quarter \(c =\) 24, the discovery quarter becomes \(c + \lfloor (d - c)(1 - r) \rfloor\) with \(r =\) 50%. This covers both events already pending at \(c\) and events that originate afterwards. Severity is drawn before the shift, so only timing changes, not the loss amount.


Exposure growth
Volume growth rises to 3% per quarter



The two example controls on the Control Value page work differently from the control-improvement scenario above. They shift the lag-distribution parameters (additively, for the event types listed in params.yaml) for the whole simulated history before severities are drawn, so a faster-detected event is also smaller through the \((1 + e \times \text{lag})\) term.

title: Late-Discovered Operational Risk Events
text:
NoteRead this first



Everything here comes from a simulation with assumed parameters, not from any firm’s data. It tests how reserving methods behave when the true answer is known. It does not estimate any real firm’s losses.

title: Late-Discovered Operational Risk Events
text:
The question
Operational losses such as trade errors, NAV pricing errors and unauthorized trading are often found long after they happen, and the loss database records them when they are found. So recent periods look cleaner than they are. This is the actuarial incurred-but-not-reported (IBNR) problem, and run-off triangles, analysed with the ChainLadder R package, are a natural way to estimate what is missing. Losses are booked in full when discovered, so this is a pure IBNR problem: it does not model later development on events already known (provisions, recoveries, insurance; see Limitations).

title: Late-Discovered Operational Risk Events
section: What we found (under the assumed generator)
text:
What we found (under the assumed generator)

Recent reported losses understate the truth, a lot for slow-to-detect events. For the latest four quarters, the share of true incurred loss not yet in the database averages 11% for trade errors, 59% for NAV errors and 87% for unauthorized trading. For unauthorized trading the typical (median) database has 100% of that loss still unrecorded, so in a typical year none of it has been found yet. (pictures below)
Standard methods work only where events are plentiful. Mack and bootstrap chain-ladder are close to unbiased for trade errors (1% and 2% relative bias) and acceptable for NAV errors (10% for Mack). Their 95% intervals are somewhat too narrow: Mack covers the truth 94% of the time for trade errors and 92% for NAV errors, while bootstrap covers 86% and 90%. (Results)
For rare, heavy-tailed unauthorized trading, the standard package implementations mostly cannot run. Mack was usable in 0 of 200 databases. That is a limit of the MackChainLadder() implementation on triangles with empty development columns. Setting those factors to 1 makes Mack run (200 of 200), but its relative bias is 866%, its median error -42% and its interval coverage 43%; Bornhuetter-Ferguson with an external development pattern is better in the median (14%) but has no interval and is unstable in the mean. A frequency x severity approach gives a usable estimate (relative bias -4%) but its 95% intervals cover only 63%. Only 2.7% of unauthorized-trading events are discovered after the 10-year window, yet they carry about 40% of the true undiscovered loss, because loss grows while an event stays hidden (up to 4.2 times the initial size at lag 40). (Results)
A control improvement fools development methods. If detection gets faster, methods trained on the slower past keep predicting development that no longer occurs. After the improvement, Mack’s mean estimate of undiscovered loss is $153.4K for trade errors against a true $94.46K, and $3.1M for NAV errors against a true $1.6M. Restricting the development factors to the latest three diagonals removes most of the trade-error gap. (Results)
Faster detection mainly buys earlier information; the dollar savings rest on one assumption. Expected annual loss is $6.0M (12 bps of a $5B firm). The two example controls save $502.30K and $735.12K a year against assumed costs of $400.0K and $700.0K: close to break-even on the mean, with 95% expected shortfall falling from $31.8M to $26.8M and $23.4M (the reduction under reconciliation automation has a paired 95% bootstrap interval of $3.0M to $7.4M). Both the mean and the tail savings exist only because simulated losses grow while undiscovered (0.02 to 0.08 per quarter in this model); with no growth both vanish. What remains is earlier information: undiscovered loss at year 10 falls from $12.6M to $6.3M and $4.5M. (Control value)

title: Late-Discovered Operational Risk Events
section: What this means for a COO or CRO (conditional on the above)
text:
What this means for a COO or CRO (conditional on the above)

Treat the most recent year of loss data for slow-detection event types as incomplete, and say so when reporting trends.
Do not apply a standard development method blindly to rare, large-loss events; use a frequency-severity view and an explicit tail assumption.
Judge a detection control by how much of its promised lag reduction it must deliver to break even, not by a single point ROI.
Check how your loss data feeds capital and compensation. For banks, the Basel III Standardised Approach (SMA) builds its Loss Component from about ten years of internal loss data, so late-discovered losses enter by date of accounting and the latest years understate exposure. For asset managers, NAV-error compensation is recognised when the error is found, so the most recent loss trend understates exposure in the same way. Confirm the exact treatment against your own regulator’s rules.

title: Late-Discovered Operational Risk Events
text:
The problem in pictures

Why recent periods look clean
A loss event database is organised by when an event was discovered, not when it happened. A trade error booked on Monday may be found by reconciliation the same week. A mispriced NAV may surface a year later. An unauthorized position can run for several years.
So at any evaluation date, the most recent origin periods have had the least time to be discovered. Their recorded losses are low because the events have not yet been found, not necessarily because controls improved. This is the same structure as incurred-but-not-reported (IBNR) claims in insurance reserving, and a run-off triangle is the natural way to see it.


One synthetic database, as a triangle
Rows are origin periods (years), columns are discovery lags (years after origin). A cell holds the loss from events that originated in that row and were discovered that many years later. The database can only fill the upper-left; the lower-right (orange) is real loss that exists but has not been discovered.








Figure 1: NAV-error losses, one simulated database, annual granularity. The orange region is known only because the data are synthetic.







The artifact: reported losses fall, true losses do not
Averaging 100 simulated databases, the figure below compares what the database reports for each origin quarter with the true incurred loss. The gap opens in the last few years and is widest for the event types with the longest detection lags.








Figure 2: Mean loss by origin quarter over 100 simulated databases: true incurred (line) vs. reported by the end of quarter 40 (area).





For the latest four origin quarters in the baseline scenario, the share of true incurred loss that is not yet in the database averages 11% for trade errors, 59% for NAV errors and 87% for unauthorized trading (median 100%). These shares depend on the assumed lag distributions (see Synthetic Data); they illustrate the mechanism, not any real firm.


What the rest of the site tests
If the missing amount can be estimated from the shape of past development, a firm can correct its recent loss figures and size a reserve-like buffer. The question we test is which estimation methods are trustworthy for which event type, using synthetic data where the true answer is known.

title: Results
text:
Dollar-loss triangles
Dollar-loss triangles are what a risk committee cares about, but they are the hard case: a single large event dominates a cell, and late-discovered events are larger.

Routes to the missing amount

Direct development methods on the dollar triangle: plain chain-ladder, Mack (the package implementation, and a version that sets development factors of empty columns to 1 so it runs on sparse triangles), Mack using only the latest three calendar diagonals, bootstrap chain-ladder, and Clark growth curves.
Bornhuetter-Ferguson (BF) and Benktander. An a-priori expected loss (loss per unit exposure, estimated from the five oldest origin years, times exposure) is weighted by the share still unreported. The share comes either from the triangle’s own chain-ladder pattern, or from an external benchmark pattern. The benchmark here is the generator’s own lag distribution, so it shows what an accurate external pattern buys and is optimistic. BF and Benktander give point estimates only.
Frequency x severity: project the number of undiscovered events from the count triangle, then price each projected event by resampling observed severities at a similar lag. This keeps the stable count signal separate from the noisy severities. It ignores parameter uncertainty, so we expect its intervals to be too narrow. A variant pools all observed severities and re-applies an estimated linear lag uplift.

Trade and NAV errors: Mack, bootstrap, Bornhuetter-Ferguson and frequency x severity are all usable and within about 15% of the truth in aggregate. Relative biases for NAV errors are Mack 10%, bootstrap 14%, BF with its own pattern 7% and frequency x severity -7%.
Package Mack versus Mack with empty-column handling. The package fails in 200 of 200 unauthorized-trading databases (non-finite development factors from empty columns). Setting those factors to 1 makes it run in 200 of them, and identical to the package where the package runs (trade and NAV errors). So the failure is an implementation limit. But the result when it runs is poor: relative bias 866%, median signed error -42% and interval coverage 43%. A single large loss in the latest diagonal is multiplied by large factors, so the mean is far too high while the typical database is underestimated.
Bornhuetter-Ferguson on unauthorized trading does not remove the problem. With its own pattern the relative bias is 70% (median -15%); with the benchmark pattern 50% (median 14%). The a-priori loss per unit exposure is itself estimated from heavy-tailed history, so one large old loss inflates every origin year. BF has no interval here.
Frequency x severity has relative bias -4% on unauthorized trading and the best coverage among methods with intervals, but only 63%. At long lags few observed events exist: 62% of projected unauthorized-trading events are priced from the all-event pool because no events are nearby in lag (median fewest donors for any lag with projected events: 2). The uplift-pooling variant has relative bias 24% and coverage 67%, so pooling does not by itself fix the under-coverage.
Recent-origin bias (relative bias for the latest origin year only) is much larger than overall bias for unauthorized trading with frequency x severity (26% against -4% overall): the most recent origin year has the largest undiscovered share, so errors concentrate there, and it is exactly the year a decision-maker cares about.
Beyond the window: about 40% of the true undiscovered unauthorized-trading loss is discovered more than 40 quarters after origin, although only 2.7% of unauthorized-trading events are (late events are scaled up by the severity-growth term). No in-window method can see it; it needs an explicit tail assumption.

Clark curves: ages are period ends (1 to 10 years), the package default for the average date of loss (half an origin period), maxage is the window length, and Cape Cod exposure is the exposure path scaled so that expected loss ratios start near 1. These conventions are the package’s own; they are not the cause of the poor trade-error results. The cause is the shape of the data. title: Results
text:
Method validation
Because the data are synthetic, every method can be scored against the true undiscovered amount. We generate 200 independent databases per scenario, fit each method to each, and record bias, error and interval coverage. A fit is usable only if the method ran and passed sanity checks. Fits that error out (failed) or return an implausible result (suspect, for example a bootstrap IBNR of zero, a bootstrap mean below 10% of the deterministic chain-ladder, or a growth-curve parameter on its optimiser bound) are excluded from bias figures. Two coverage columns are shown: coverage among usable fits, and coverage over all fits where failed, suspect and interval-free fits count as misses. Rows with fewer than 20 usable fits are shown as a dash.

No method is reliable for every event type. The ranking changes with how many events there are and how heavy their tails are.

Stress tests
Chain-ladder methods assume that the pattern of past development carries forward. Five scenarios break that assumption, or the data-generating assumptions, in different ways. All use annual triangles and the same 200 seeds as the baseline (the scenario index is part of the seed, so each scenario has its own databases).

Why it is hard

Two very large unauthorized-trading losses are injected; one is discovered, one is not yet (table below)

Detection gets faster partway through, so history over-predicts future development

Rising volume distorts comparisons across origin periods

Negative-binomial counts (same mean as baseline, larger variance)

What the stress tests show

Control improvement. After detection speeds up, the true undiscovered trade-error amount falls from $185.0K to $94.5K, about half. Methods trained on the earlier, slower history keep projecting the old development: Mack’s mean estimate is $153.4K, 62% too high. A firm that has just improved its controls will over-reserve if it applies old development factors. Restricting the factors to the latest three diagonals removes most of the error here ($96.2K against the truth) and reduces it for NAV errors ($2.1M against $1.6M), at the price of noisier factors in the other scenarios (4% bias and 88% coverage for trade errors in the baseline, against 1% and 94%). It does not help unauthorized trading. The calendar-diagonal test is weak on 10 x 10 annual triangles: it flags the change in 32% of trade-error databases and 12% of NAV-error databases, against about 0% false alarms in the baseline. A change that the test cannot see on annual data can still be large enough to matter.
Heavy-tail shock. For unauthorized trading, frequency x severity has relative bias -33% and interval coverage 94%. BF with a benchmark pattern is close in aggregate (11%), and plain chain-ladder is wildly high because the injected losses are multiplied by large development factors. One injected loss is discovered inside the realised history and one is not (table above), so part of the truth is information the severity pool never contained.
Exposure growth. Moderate growth changes little for the event types where the methods already work.
Overdispersion. Interval coverage falls for the methods that have intervals: Mack covers 90% of trade-error databases and bootstrap 78%, against 94% and 86% in the baseline. Clustered or overdispersed counts make the stated 95% intervals less trustworthy.
Reporting threshold. A $10k threshold removes most trade errors from the database (the true undiscovered trade-error amount falls from $185.0K to $80.0K) while NAV errors and unauthorized trading are barely affected; for trade and NAV errors the standard methods still work on what remains (unauthorized-trading means are dominated by a few databases and vary a lot between scenarios).

title: Control Value
text: Faster detection has value because (i) loss is recorded sooner, which improves information, and (ii) in this simulator an event’s size grows linearly with the time it stays undiscovered, through the factor \((1 + e \times \text{lag})\). Channel (ii) is the only way a control changes incurred loss; if \(e = 0\), mean and tail incurred loss are identical with and without the control, and only the information value in (i) remains. This page measures how much a detection control is worth under those assumptions. The effect sizes and costs are placeholders, not benchmarks; a real engagement would replace them with measured detection times and quoted prices.

title: Control Value
text:
Information value
The cleanest benefit that does not depend on severity growth is earlier information. At the evaluation date, the loss that has already happened but is not yet in the database falls from $12.6M to $6.3M under reconciliation automation and $4.5M under independent P&L verification. A smaller undiscovered balance means the reported loss trend is closer to the true one, and the loss data a firm uses for capital, board reporting or allocator disclosure is less incomplete. This benefit is not converted to dollars here, because its value depends on how the firm uses the data.

title: Control Value
text:
Caveats specific to this page

Incurred loss changes under a control only through the severity-growth term \((1 + e \times \text{lag})\). If losses do not grow while undiscovered (\(e = 0\)), neither the mean nor the tail of incurred loss changes; the only benefit left is earlier information, shown above as undiscovered loss at year 10.
Control cost is a single annual figure with no ramp-up, no false-positive workload and no risk of the control failing.
Losses are gross. Loss-event insurance, recoveries from counterparties and compensation that is later clawed back would reduce net losses and therefore net savings.
No discounting, no correlation with market stress, and no regulatory or reputational effects are modelled.
